ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
 Pending projects for Rail Safety  
*61. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be -
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several projects related to Rail safety in 
terms of track renewal rolling stock replacement/repair >f Railway bridges 
are pending; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof, date-wise and Zone-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): a) and 
(b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Renewal and replacement of tracks, bridges and rolling stock a 
continuous ongoing exercise. The works under these items are auctioned 
every year through the budget on the basis of laid down 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
criteria. For such replacements the sanctioned works are progressed and 
completed in a phased manner as per availability of funds and resources. 
As on 1.4.2002, the position of Track Renewal, Bridge works and 
Rolling Stock Programme has been as under: 
Track Renewal—Works are sanctioned for total 14,509 km. of track, 
out of which 4,000 km. is targeted for completion during 2002-2003. 
Bridges— A total of 4481 Nos. of bridges, including 527 distressed, are 
sanctioned and 1010 Nos. including 341 distressed bridges, are targeted for 
completion during the year 2002-03. 
Rolling Stock —No projects are pending for replacement of rolling 
stock, since rolling stock is not replaced based on projects but on the basis of 
Production Plan which is drawn up every year taking into account the 
fluctuations in traffic requirements and rolling stock replacement requirement 
on age cum condition basis. The actual production as per plan, is achieved on 
year to year basis. The figures, for the current year, are given below:

SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the detailed reply given 
by the hon. Railway Minister should actually be an eye-opener to the whole 
country because the kind of work that is remaining incomplete or unfinished 
is stupendous. The fact that we are not having more accidents of a fatal nature 
and some passengers are actually surviving the ordeal of journey on the 
Indian Railways is some kind of a mi racle. So far as track renewal is 
concerned, works were sanctioned for 14,509 km. of track, of which 4,000 
km. of track is targeted for completion during 2002-03. So far as the bridges 
which are to be repaired and renewed are concerned, sanction was given for 
4,481 bridges of which 1,010 bridges were targeted for completion during the 
year 2002-03. Apart from the accident involving the Howrah Rajdhani 
Express, many other train accidents have taken place. We are hearing almost 
on a daily basis that this or that train had a miraculous escape. At the last 
moment, something is identified; either there is some problem with the track 
or there is some problem with the bridge or there is some problem with the 
signal. The Khanna Committee which went into the question of railway safety 
in a big 
                                               3

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
way had made a number of recommendations. The main issue which was 
pointed out by the Khanna Committee was that there was no safety policy of 
the Railways. In such a situation, the Government of India made a major 
exception and Rs. 17,000 crores over a period of five years were earmarked 
for railway safety. Although this figure of Rs. 17,000 crores appears to be 
very impressive, but year-wise it is only Rs. 1,400 crores, Rs. 2,000 crores and 
so on. In this kind of a situation, the urgency or the importance that had to be 
shown by the Government in terms of reinforcing the safety measures, has not 
been shown. It is not that we do not have the resources or we cannot address 
the problem of safety wholly. But, the remaining part is very huge compared 
to the requirements. All other resources, which were available with the 
Railways, should have been diverted towards safety measures. My question is 
this. Woulcf the Government come up with a proper railway safety policy 
statement and also a White Paper along with an investment plan on an urgent 
basis, so that Parliament could have an opportunity to discuss it and 
recommend certain measures, thereby we are able to fulfil the safety 
requirements?

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the hon. Minister is 
correct when he says that Rs.17,000 crores earmarked for safety are not being 
diverted. It is not a question of compartmentalisation of resources. It is a 
question of availability of the total resources and prioritisation by the 
Railways. It could be creation of new zones, or, safety that may be the 
priority. I understand the predicament of the hon. Railway Minister that 
whenever he presents a Budget, all of us, be it Members sitting on this side or 
on that side, demand that there should be a new train, or, a new connection or 
a new line, completely ignoring that the resources available are limited. 
Within the limited resources available, what your priority is. That is the moot 
question. If Rs.17,000 crores are made available to you, from the figures that 
you have given, I have calculated that even the committed programmes will

Central Teams have visited all the above States except Kerala. All the 
Teams have submitted their reports. In case of Kerala the State Government 
has been requested to furnish further information and clarifications. 
It is estimated that the loss of production in kharif foodgrains 
production will be of the order of 18.72 per cent. Shortage of fodder and 
drinking water is also being experienced in many States, States have taken 
many steps to deal with the situation including initiation of relief works, 
provision of drinking water including its transport through Rail in Rajasthan, 
setting up of fodder depots, remission of land revenue and in many cases 
stocking of foodgrains at the village level. Certain States have suspended 
recovery of co-operative dues and not resorting to coercive measures to effect 
recovery. Power supply for a minimum period and seed subsidy for growing 
fodder etc. are some other notable steps taken by the State Government.

Statement 
(a) to (e) Drought is a slow on-set phenomenon showing improvements 
and aggravations in its protracted course depending on occurrence of many 
events. Keeping these factors in view, it would be pre-mature to assess 
whether the assistance provided is adequate. 
So far, Rs. 1227.29 crores of Central share of the Calamity Relief 
Fund(CRF) for 2002-2003 and 19.25 lakh MTs of foodgrains for carrying out 
relief employment works have been sanctioned. Further, an amount of Rs. 
1999.14 crores has been found admissible for assistance from National 
Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) subject to adjustment of balances in the 
Calamity Relief Fund of the States. The situation will be further reviewed in 
middle of January to assess the requirements of further assistance. The 
relevant details are in the Statement-I (See below). 
Provision of relief on the ground is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments concerned. The Central Government supplements these 
.efforts. No specific complaints of relief not reaching the affected population 
have so far been received.

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
A Statement is laid pn the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a ) and (b) The low share of India's presence in the global trade of 
medicinal plants could be attributed to poor quality of produce, Unorganized 
production and marketing system, lack of awareness and inadequate 
database. A Task Force on Conservation and Sustainable Use of Medicinal 
Plants constituted by the Planning Commission has identified the following 
bottlenecks in the development of medicinal plants: 
1. The medicinal plants are collected mostly from the wild without 
paying attention to the stage of maturity, stored haphazardly for 
long period of time under unsuitable conditions thereby causing 
deterioration in the quality which are not acceptable to importers 
and standard drug manufacturing Units. 
2. The marketing of Medicinal Plants is inefficient, informal, 
secretive and opportunistic. As a result, raw material supply 
situation is shaky, unsustainable and exploitative. This results in 
depletion of resource base, exploitation of rural people, 
adulteration and non-availability of quality herbal drugs for 
domestic consumption as well as for exports. 
3. As forest.habitats disappear and overharvesting for  commercial 
use reduces the stocks of wild medicinal plant material, there is a 
corresponding drop in the availability of the plants normally used 
as the first and last resort for all health care by rural population. 
4. Despite the wealth of resources available, the sector has not 
developed owing to the absence of suitable standardization, 
quality control and efficacy of drugs. It has yet to formalize and 
organize marketing and trade and integrate the development of 
medicinal plants form production to consumption to boost export 
of herbal formulations. 
29 

RAJYA  SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
5. The medicinal plants sector has a number of stakeholders having 
divergent interests. There is lack of coordination and each 
stakeholder is interested in strengthening specific aspects of his 
sector only and ignoring the overall development. 
6. Several constraints exist due to inadequate awareness; inadequate 
investments in research and development; manufacturer — 
exporter dissonance; lack of quality and standardization norms; 
and lack of adequate marketing and trade information. 
The Central Government have taken various initiatives to promote 
Research and Development of medicinal plants in the country including 
creation of infrastructure for quality testing. The following agencies are 
involved in encouraging the farmers to use the latest technologies for getting 
higher yield and deriving higher income: 
(i) The National Research Centre on Medicinal and Aromatic Plants, 
Anand, Gujarat under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research 
(ICAR) is carrying out research work exclusively on medicinal 
and aromatic plants. 
(ii) Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and its 
constituent laboratories including Central Institute of Medicinal 
and Aromatic Plants (CIMAP) are also carrying our research 
activities for the development of these plants. 
(iii) Department of Agriculture and Cooperation, Ministry of 
Agriculture is implementing developmental programmes on 
medicinal and aromatic plants through Plan Scheme to address the 
issues of quality planting material, conservation of germplasm, 
coverage of area under improved varieties and quality assessment 
through Regional Analytical Laboratories. 
(iv) National Medicinal Plants Board, Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare is implementing various programmes in an integrated  
manner and is overseeing the  overall

International decade for culture of peace and non-violence 
*64. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU) : Will the 
Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in view of the United Nations' declaring 2001—2010 as the 
International decade for a culture of peace and non-violence for the children 
of the World, Government have drawn out elaborate programmes for the 
children of India; and 
32 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken or proposed to be taken 
in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) The General Assembly of the 
United Nations proclaimed the year 2000 as the "International Year for the 
Culture of Peace" and the decade 2001—2010 as the uInternational Decade 
for the Promotion of a Culture of Peace and Non-Violence for the Children of 
the World'. UNESCO was entrusted with the task of mobilizing Member 
States and Associate Members and co-ordinating the programme and activities 
of the United Nations Agencies and other International Organizations. 
Accordingly UNESCO requested all National Commissions to undertake a 
series of activities which could contribute to spreading the message of 'Culture 
of Peace'. The year was formally launched world wide on 14.9.1999 which 
was the opening day of the last Session of the UN General Assembly in the 
20th Century and was designated as International day of Peace. 
The Culture of Peace and Non-Violence is not something new to our 
country. Bearing this in mind, The Indian National Commission launched the 
year with a function where Education Secretary gave an address on 'Culture of 
Peace' and the famous classical dancer Ms. Sonal Mansingh gave a 
performance on the theme of Peace before an International audience and the 
guests signed the Culture of Peace manifesto. All-the State Governments, 
Associated Schools, UNESCO Clubs, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and 
Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan were also requested to organize activities on 
the Culture of Peace and to sign the Culture of Peace Manifesto. The 
Manifesto was also signed by the Prime Minister at a simple ceremony at 
P.M. House. Apart from the activities undertaken by the State Governments, 
Associated Schools, UNESCO Clubs, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and 
Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan a major International Youth Forum on 
Cultural Heritage was jointly organized from 28th December, 2000 to 2nd 
January, 2001 by the Indian National Commission and the Delhi Public 
School, R. K. Puram. In addition, the Indian National Commission organized 
10 Workshops on the Culture of Peace at Gurgaon, Faridabad, Shimla, 
Dehradun, Jammu, Patna, Kolasib, Bhopal, Pataudi and Delhi with a view to 
associating 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
the NGOs, students and UNESCO Clubs etc. with the Culture of Peace 
movement. 
On the recommendation of the Indian National Commission the 
Brahma Kumar’s signed an agreement with UNESCO for participation in the 
movement. By employing a Task Force of four thousands volunteers over a 
period of 7 months they collected over 35 million signatures in India alone 
for the Manifesto of Culture of Peace. 
A UNESCO Chair on Culture of Peace and Non-Violence has been 
functioning since 1999 at the Manipal Academy of Higher Education, 
Manipal. 
As regards the "International Decade for the Promotion of a Culture of 
Peace and Non-Violence for the Children of the World' each year is required 
to be marked with a different priority and for 2001, UNESCO had suggested 
that the emphasis be given to the United Nations Year of Dialogue among 
Civilizations and the International year of Mobilization against Racism, 
Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and related Intolerance. During the 
UNESCO's General Conference held in October-November, 2001 the 
President of the Indian National Commission conveyed India's intention to 
organize an International Conference on Dialogue among Civilizations, which 
was accepted by the Director General. Further details for organizing the 
Conference are being worked out. 
The Commission is organising a series of lectures in connection with 
the "International Decade for the Promotion of a Culture of Peace and Non-
Violence for the Children of the World'. Two such lectures-one by His 
Holiness the Dalai Lama and the other by Acharya Vidyanandji Muniraj were 
organized during the last year. 
The City Montessori School, Lucknow has been awarded the UNESCO 
Prize for Peace Education for 2002 "in recognition of its efforts to promote 
the universal values of education for peace and tolerance and to renew the 
principles of secularism at a time when these values and principles are 
increasingly being challenged."

(c) what are the suggestions made by the Indian Government in the 
above Convention; and 
(d) whether Government propose to implement it? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T .R. 
BAALU) (a) to (d) The Eighth Conference of the Parties to the United Nations 
Framework Convention on Climate Change was held recently in New Delhi 
from 23rd October to 1st November 2002. The Delhi Ministerial Declaration 
on Climate Change and Sustainable Development issued at the end of the 
Conference establishes the link between climate change and sustainable 
development and brings into focus the issue of adaptation to the adverse 
effects of climate change. The Conference advanced operationalisation of 
Special Climate Change Fund and Least Developed Countries Fund for providing 
financial resources to developing countries. The Conference also concluded 
three years of negotiations relating to reporting and review under the Kyoto 
Protocol and rules of procedure of Executive Board of the Clean Development 
Mechanism as well as simplified modalities and procedures for small-scale 
Clean Development Mechanism projects. It also adopted the New Delhi Work 
programme relating to education, training and public awareness about issues 
relating to climate change. 
A group of developed countries wanted to initiate a process for 
beginning a dialogue on broader participation of countries in greenhouse 
92 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
gas mitigation commitments for period beyond 2012. This was resisted 
successfully by the developing countries, including India, on the grounds that the 
per capita greenhouse gas emissions of the developing countries, in general, were 
low in comparison to the developed countries, and that the overriding priority for 
the developing countries was poverty eradication for which economic growth 
was essential. A framework of legislative and policy measures are in place in 
India that would help in minimizing the causes of climate change. Several 
measures have already been implemented by the Government of India to 
promote efficient utilization of fossil fuels, use of renewable energy 
technologies, abatement of pollution and conservation of forests. 
Johannesburg Earth Summit 
373. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the major issues considered by the UN World Summit on 
Sustainable Development (the Earth Summit) held in Johannesburg recently; 
(b) the assessment of the progress made on various issues since the last 
Summit at Rio de Janeiro in 1992, with highlights of the contentious issues 
involved and the Indian view point thereon; and 
(c) the final resolutions adopted by the Summit and the follow up action 
required to be taken by India? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU) (a) World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) acted as a 
10-year review of the United Nations Conference on Environment and 
Development (UNCED) process and identified major accomplishments and 
obstacles in implementing Agenda 21. The major issues considered by the 
WSSD, inter-alia, include poverty eradication, changing unsustainable patterns 
of consumption and production, protecting and managing the natural resource 
base of economic and social development, sustainable development in a 
globalizing world, health and sustainable development, sustainable 
development of small island developing countries, means of implementation 
and institutional framework for sustainable development. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
(b) The major outcome of the Summit was that it reaffirmed 
"sustainable development" as a central element of the international 
agenda and gave a new impetus on global action to fight poverty and 
protect the environment. The understanding of sustainable development 
was broadened and strengthened as a result of the Summit, particularly 
important linkages between poverty, the environment and the use of 
natural resources were clearly established. As a result of a coordinated 
approach adopted by the developing countries including India, in addition 
to reiterating Millennium Development Goals and objectives of various 
multilateral environment agreements the Summit agreed on: 
(i) Increasing the number of people with access to clean water and 
sanitation facilities by half by the year 2015. 
(ii) Reducing the proportion of people without access to cleaner energy 
by the year 2015. 
(iii) Helping the developing countries with necessary resources to 
increase the share of renewable energy in a gradual manner. 
(iv) Evolving an international regime to ensure fair and equitable 
sharing of benefits arising from the use of genetic resources in a 
transparent manner. 
(v) Developed Countries to take lead in shifting away from the present 
pattern of unsustainable consumption and production. 
(vi) Successfully countered the efforts made by various blocks on 
imposing disguised trade barriers in the nature of eco-labeling, life-
cycle analysis criteria, and inclusion of core labour standards of ILO. 
(c) The Plan of Implementation and Political Declaration issued 
after the Summit has highlighted concerns of developing countries and 
reflect consensus among all countries arrived after the WSSD. The Plan 
of Implementation calls for immediate international action to tackle 
these issues. The Government regularly monitors its performance on 
the benchmark of annual and Five Year Plans which contain all elements 
of sustainable development. Ministry of Environment and Forests has 
set up a mechanism for follow up action on various decisions taken in 
the World Summit.

CHAPTER 4 
Modernisation of Signal and Telecommunication System 
4. Highlights 
 The Standing Committee on Railways (1996) viewed that the

Railways should be made a thrust area for investment in IXth Plan 
(1997—2002). However, during the period from 1996-97 to 2000-01, 
out of the total allocation of Rs. 58010.96 crore on nine Zonal 
Railways for Grant No. 16—Assets, Acquisition, Construction and 
Replacement, the allocation for S&T was only Rs. 1482.02 crore, a 
mere 2.55 per cent. 
(Para 6) 
146 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
 Modernisation of points and signals through Panel Interlocking . 
(PI), Route Relay Interlocking (RRI) and Solid State Interlocking 
(SSI) had not been completed. Out of 5244 signalling stations, 
only 1812,180 and 13 stations respectively were provided with 
PI, RRI and SSI and 3093 stations were still being operated 
mechanically. In 431 out of 1075 stations on 'A' route, points 
and signals are still being operated through mechanical means. 
(Para 7.1) 
 Out of 6746.73 route Km, automatic signalling was in use only for a 
limited length i.e. in 560.34 route Kms. on 'A' route and work was 
stated to be in progress on 170 route Kms. No concrete steps had been 
taken to introduce modern signalling system on remaining 6016.39 
route Kms. of 'A' route. 
(Para 7.2)

railways, where the utilization of line capacity is more than 100% 
automatic block signalling has not been provided to de-congest the 
traffic. 
(Para 7.2.1.1) 
 Sanction for construction of 3rd line was accorded during the 
review period in 8 sections on three Zonal Railway at a cost of

increase cogld have been achieved by provision of automatic 
block signalling at an estimated cost of Rs. 61.42 crores. 
(Para 7.2.1.2) 
 Due to line capacity constraints, traffic on 17 routes is being 
moved through longer routes for mo re than five years. In respect 
of 8 routes, rationalization orders were in force for more than 10

Experiments about monsoon failure 
449. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Indian Meteorological Department's experts have 
examined the causes for the failure of the just concluded summer monsoon in 
the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the results of experiment conducted jointly by several 
organisations in the Arabian Sea between June, 15 and August, 15 to gather 
ocean and atmospheric observations have been examined; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the measures to be adopted for long range month-wise 
prediction of the Monsoon in future? 
157 

RAJYA  SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY ( SHRI BHACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) to (e) The Indian 
Meteorological Department has examined the causes of failure of this year's 
monsoon. This year, the onset of the southwest monsoon over Kerala was on 
time (29 May). It covered peninsular India, northeast region and some parts of 
east central India by middle of June, as per its normal pattern. The rainfall 
activity was normal (+7%) during June. This was caused mainly by the 
development of a low pressure area that moved westward across central parts 
of the country. Thereafter, there was delay in its further progress. Dry spells 
and breaks in the monsoon are the normal features of the monsoon system. 
This year, however, the break in the monsoon developed even before its 
advance over north/northwest India resulting in prolonged dry summer 
conditions. The details of the failure of Monsoon 2002 are as follow:— 
(i) The delay in the progression of monsoon was due to the presence 
of an anomalous anticyclonic flow/descending motion over 
western parts of country. 
(ii) Heavy rainfall events are in association with monsoon depressions 
which develop over Bay of Bengal during monson season. Not a 
single monsoon depression formed during this season as against 
the normal of 5-6 depressions per season. 
(iii) Most of low pressure areas formed during the season we/e quite 
feeble. They were short lived and moved along the seasonal 
trough. 
(iv) The seasonal/monsoon trough itself had been quite weak and was 
located close to foothills of Himalayas for a long time in July. 
(v) The cross equatorial flow in the Arabian Sea as well as in the Bay 
of Bengal was extremely weak. Cloud system moved towards 
pacific Ocean particularly during the month of July and in the 
second half of September. 
158 

[22 November, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(vi) The El-Nino showed an anomalous behaviour in that, it weakened 
over the area off Peru coast during monsoon season but 
strengthened over West Pacific Ocean. 
The Department of Science and Technology (DST) is coordinating the 
Arabian Sea Monsoon Experiment (ARMEX) under Indian Climate Research 
Programme (ICRP) in two phases. The first phase was organised from 15 
June to 15 August this year with the participation of a large number of 
national organisations. In order to understand development of small scale 
heavy rain producing systems associated with Offshore trough/vortex 
attempts were made to gather atmospheric and oceanic observations which 
were maximised during 'Intensive Observation Period'. These observations are 
being currently analysed by all the participating agencies. The second phase 
of ARMEX will be conducted from mid March to mid May 2003, in which 
observations will be collected to understand the development and collapse of 
warm pool in southeast Arbian Sea. The total picture will emerge only after 
the second phase is over. 
Action has been initiated to develop the forecast models for the month-
wise prediction of monsoon rainfall.

which as all of us know is many areas they have all been taken over and 
houses have been constructed in the rural areas also. We have to consider 
both these things. As the Prime Minister had announced in the Lok Sabha, a 
scheme of linking rivers is under the activities consideration of the 
Government. We will look into it. Money will not be a hindrance in 
implementing that plan, if that can be done technically. 
I come back to the PDS and other things. Let me make one thing very 
clear. The Central Government can only have schemes and can give money. 
The Central Government has no implementing agency. We do not have 
patwaris; we do not have SDMs and we do not have District Collectors under 
our control. We have no implementing agency and monitoring agency. After 
all, they are democratically elected Governments. We can give them money. 
We can give them assistance. We can tell them what to do. But it is their right 
to decide how they should use that money and how effectively they should 
spend that money. Therefore, if you say that the Central Government should 
be held responsible if food is not distributed properly or if the money 
intended does not reach the people for whom it is intended. I don't think in 
our federal system that is the right way of putting things. 
Many hon. Members wanted that the elected representatives should be 
associated with the draught relief work. This demand was

merchants of Thiruvannamalai, it should be prevented.

the temple. They want to worship the deity, the sanctum. In Tamil Nadu, at 
Valluvarkottam, the statue of Valluvar, Pomhukkar, Kannagi are being 
neglected. The Archaeological Survey of India is taking steps to take this 
temple in its custody. Therefore, it is requested that respecting the sentiments 
of the people of Tamil Nadu, the hon. Prime Minister should intervene in the 
matter and prevent this from happening.

countries. Such violence continues to cut across culture,

class, education, income, ethnicity and age. Domestic violence is one of the most

Sir, the domestic violence in India is no less than cancer or any other 
ailment. But there is no law to protect its victims. Not a day passes when

SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominated): Thank you, Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir. I will just take a few minutes, not only to welcome this Private 
Member's Bill, but also to emphasise to all the Members in this House that the 
right to the matrimonial home, what is called the shared household, as the Bill 
describes it, is the most important insurance against domestic violence. This 
concept, Sir, was an invention, originally, of Judges in England. After the War, 
when half a million soldiers did not come back because they were killed in 
France, Germany etc., there were a large number of widows in England who 
were subjected to eviction proceedings. These eviction proceedings resulted 
in eviction orders, because the tenant was only the husband and since there 
were no prospects of the husband coming back, the court said: "An eviction 
order has to go, as a matter of course." So, thousands and thousands 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2002] 
of widows were evicted, and it was only because of the ingenuity of a 
great Judge, Lord Denning, particularly, who invented this concept of a 
matrimonial home that the women were saved. He said that the 
matrimonial home is a concept which we must now introduce in society, 
namely, the husband and the wife share a home and therefore, this 
shared household concept came in. Unfortunately, this decision was 
reversed by the House of Lords. They said: "When we look at the law, 
there is no such thing here," and there was such an uproar in Parliament 
that they had to introduce a Bill, which became the Matrimonial Homes 
Act. Therefore, Sir, I very strongly recommend to the hon. Minister to 
consider that in the Government-int roduced Bill, where this clause is 
absent. It is a very, very important protection, almost a certain insurance, 
against domestic violence, and I would respectfully request the 
Government to kindly introduce this concept in such form as they think 
right, because it is time we introduced it. It was introduced long ago in 
the European countries. We must now introduce it in our society. 
Secondly, the term domestic violence as the hon. Member, Mr. Santosh 
Bagrodia, when he spoke from the floor said, was inadequately defined. 
Right. It was inadequately defined, but I would respectfully suggest, let 
us not reinvent the wheel. It has been considered very carefully and the 
U.N. Model Code of Conduct on Violence defines domestic violence. 
So, I would respectfully suggest that, as far as possible, we adopt that 
provision to our definition of domestic violence because it covers a 
very wide variety of different types of violence. It is correct that we 
require a change in the mindset because we are a male-dominated 
society. But laws do help and laws do bring about a social change and 
help establish norms of behaviour. And ultimately we must try to break 
this chain of violence where the frustrations of a daughter-in-law lead 
to a dominant mother-in-law, who herself becomes violent to her daughter-
in-law in turn because that is also a type of violence that we have to 
eschew, that we have to prevent and that requires certainly, as one of 
the honourable Members rightly said, education in our society, in this 
particularly male-dominated society. But I would respectfully urge that 
even if the honourable Minister does not accept all the provisions of 
this Bill, the two most important provisions are: (1) The proper definition 
of 'domestic violence', and (2) The right to a shared household, 
howsoever you put it, or a matrimonial home. Thank you.

The Constitution (Amendment) Bill, 1999 (Insertion of 
 New Article 21A) 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Sir, I move:— 
"That the Bill further to amend the Constitution of India, be taken into 
consideration". 
Sir, for a human being, privacy is very important factor. Today, what is 
happening is that, whoever is the authority, just gets into your house thinking 
that they can take advantage of a particular clause of a Bill. It is so 
unfortunate that on flimsy grounds, on mere assumptions, they get into your 
houses; not only your houses, but the houses of your relations, distant 
relations, distant friends. I also know that in some cases, these authorities have 
entered our multi-storeyed building, going into every flat of the multi-storeyed 
building. Now, that is not privacy. After all, the dignity of an individual 
should be respected. We are in a society where freedom is very important. And 
If my privacy is hampered, if my privacy is questioned, then it becomes a 
police raj. It would mean as if we are in a situation where the entire country is 
made of scoundrels. And it is only the officers, only the bureaucrats, only a 
small number of intelligence officers or other officers in different departments, 
economic or other departments, who are most honest, who are absolutely 
above board. This is not fair. This has to be looked into by the Government very 
seriously to see how we can protect the dignity of an ordinary citizen. I know 
a number of people, a number of officers just getting into somebody's house, 
saying that they have got the right, that they will bring out some paper, etc. It 
has been noticed that, sometimes they sign the warrant on the spot, and when 
they enter, they donl allow the people to take the help of the lawyers. An 
ordinary citizen is not supposed to be an expert lawyer; he is not an expert on 
law matters. He is told "No, sorry", because that is the only way you can 
threaten him.
